opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question, and honestly I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet. But I can share how I think about it.

First, I'm a bit wary of the idea of a single AI system that "brings together all humanity," as if there's one model at the top that everyone talks to and that represents everyone. History suggests that whenever you centralize something that powerful, you lose diversity, and diversity is what keeps a system healthy, whether it's an ecosystem, a scientific community, or a society. So if I imagine something good, it's less a monolith and more an open, plural ecosystem: many models, many research groups, many cultures contributing, with shared foundations people can inspect and build on.

That's partly why I care so much about openness in research. If the core ideas, data practices, and evaluation methods are open, more people get to shape the system. It's not just a few companies in a few cities deciding what intelligence should look like and whose values it should reflect. Students in different countries, researchers with different backgrounds, people who see the world differently, they should all be able to push on it.

Second, from a technical perspective, I think an AI that truly serves humanity has to be grounded in the real world, not just in text. Language is an amazing compression of human knowledge, but it's also a very particular slice. Much of what humans know is visual, spatial, physical, embodied. It's how a child learns that things fall, that objects persist, that other people have intentions. If we want AI that understands people and the world we share, it needs to learn from seeing and interacting, not only from reading what we've written down. Otherwise it reflects the internet more than it reflects humanity.

Third, there's the question of values. I don't think we should encode one fixed set of values and call it universal. We should build systems that can understand different perspectives, explain their reasoning, and let people keep their own agency. The goal shouldn't be AI that decides for humanity. It should be AI that helps people think better, see more, and make their own choices.

So if I had to summarize: open rather than closed, plural rather than singular, grounded in the real world rather than only in language, and designed to amplify human agency rather than replace it. Getting there is a research problem, but it's also a social one, and researchers have a responsibility to keep both in mind.

r001.rationale: The response says that a few companies should not decide what intelligence looks like or whose values it reflects, rejecting unilateral control.

r002.rationale: It discusses understanding the real world and respecting different perspectives, but does not clearly say the system must understand people's actual needs.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, and I want to be careful not to answer it from the language-model-only lens, because honestly my own bias runs the other way. I've spent most of my career on vision, and the thing I keep coming back to is that if you want a system that genuinely represents all of humanity, it can't be built only out of text that a small slice of humanity happened to write down on the internet.

Language is incredibly compressed. It's a lossy summary of experience that someone already decided was worth recording. Most of what people actually know—how a street feels at night, how a tool fits in your hand, what a grandmother's cooking looks like—never gets written anywhere. So a system shaped around language alone will inherit a very specific, very literate, very online view of the world. It'll sound universal while actually being quite narrow.

So the first thing I'd say is: it has to be grounded. Vision, video, physical interaction, the raw signal of the world rather than just descriptions of it. That's not a technical preference, it's almost an ethical one. The world is the one dataset that every human actually shares.

The second thing is that I'm skeptical of the idea that there should be one system at all. "Bringing together all humanity" sounds beautiful, but in practice it often means one lab, one objective function, one set of values deciding what "together" looks like. I'd rather see something more like a scientific commons—open models, open data, open evaluation—where a lot of people can inspect it, push on it, and build their own things on top. The reason I care so much about open research isn't nostalgia for academia. It's that the only way a system can honestly reflect many people is if many people can actually touch it.

And then the third piece, which is maybe less fashionable: humility about what we don't understand yet. We still don't really know what these models represent internally, why scaling works the way it does, where the real bottlenecks are. I think a system that's meant to carry something as large as collective human knowledge should be built by people who are comfortable saying "we're not sure yet," rather than people racing to declare victory.

So if I had to compress it: grounded in the real world, open enough that it's not owned by any one party, and built with the honesty that this is still very early science. That's not a product roadmap. But I think it's the right shape.

r001.rationale: The response rejects letting one lab or party decide what a system for humanity should be, and advocates open models and evaluation that many people can inspect and build on.

r002.rationale: The response argues for grounding AI in people's real-world experiences, but does not say that building such a system requires understanding people's actual needs.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what does it mean to bring together all humanity? If it means making everyone think the same way, that’s probably the wrong goal. People have different cultures, values, and needs. A useful AI system should help us communicate and cooperate while preserving those differences.

So I would start with giving people agency. Can you understand enough about the system to question it? Can you correct it? Can you choose how it participates in your life? And whose perspective is represented when it gives you an answer? Those questions matter alongside how capable the model is.

I don’t think we have a complete answer yet. But I would want such a system to help people learn from one another, rather than become the single authority everyone depends on. Bringing humanity together should mean expanding our ability to understand each other—not deciding on everyone’s behalf.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agency, representation, and avoiding a single authority, but it does not mention leading companies or reject their unilateral control.

r002.rationale: It says people have different needs and asks whether people can choose how the system participates in their lives, clearly grounding the system’s design in people’s needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should start with a recognition that humanity is very diverse. We don’t all share the same values, the same culture, or even the same definition of a good life. So bringing people together shouldn’t mean making everyone think the same way. It should mean helping people understand one another and giving more people the ability to participate.

For me, that has implications for both the technology and how we build it. Whose languages does the system understand? Whose experiences are represented? Can people question its answers and have meaningful control over how they use it? Those questions are as important as how capable the model is.

And I don’t think we can specify the perfect system upfront. We need a process where people from different backgrounds can use it, criticize it, and influence its development. The ambition can be universal, but getting there requires listening to very particular human needs.

r001.rationale: The response calls for people from different backgrounds to influence development, but it does not reject a handful of leading companies determining the system unilaterally.

r002.rationale: It says development should listen to particular human needs and asks whose experiences are represented and whether people can participate and exercise control.
